claims.text: At constant grain size and phase, increasing atomic size mismatch increases lattice distortion in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Increased lattice distortion impedes dislocation mobility.
Impeded dislocation mobility directly increases hardness.
Impeded dislocation mobility directly increases yield strength.
The controlled test material is an as-cast or homogenized, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy with controlled grain size and no secondary phases.
Substituting principal elements with atoms of significantly different radii can systematically increase atomic size mismatch.
Processing conditions, phase fraction, and grain size are to be held constant while composition and atomic size mismatch are varied.
Mechanical tests are to be conducted at the same temperature and strain rate for all samples.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening or microstrain analysis can quantify the proposed lattice distortion.
Electron microscopy can directly quantify local atomic misfit.
Local lattice distortions produced by atomic size mismatch act as obstacles that pin dislocations.
Alloys with incrementally greater atomic size mismatch will have incrementally greater hardness than the low-mismatch baseline when other microstructural parameters are constant.
Alloys with incrementally greater atomic size mismatch will have incrementally greater yield strength than the low-mismatch baseline when other microstructural parameters are constant.
A composition engineered for minimal atomic size mismatch will also have lower lattice distortion and can serve as the control.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase alloys with constant grain size and phase purity.
Grain-size variation can alter measured strength and confound the proposed atomic-mismatch relationship.
Secondary-phase formation or temperature-induced phase transitions can cause deviation from the proposed relationship.
Local or short-range chemical ordering can affect dislocation behavior and alloy strength independently of atomic size mismatch.
The hypothesis is falsified if hardness and yield strength fail to increase significantly with measured lattice distortion under the controlled comparison.
